August 14, 2026
The Maine Department of Agriculture, Conservation and Forestry (DACF) is opening applications for the Natural Resources Disaster Relief Assistance Program (NRDRAP) today, Friday, August 14, 2026.
Maine farmers, forestry businesses, aquaculture producers, and other eligible producers who experienced weather-related losses in 2023 or 2024 may qualify for financial assistance.
Eligible losses may include crop loss, aquaculture loss, standing timber loss, harvested timber loss, on-farm and forestry infrastructure loss, and bare-ground practices necessary to mitigate land loss.
Application period
: August 14, 2026, through November 6, 2026.

Hello, this is Governor Janet Mills, and thank you for listening.

Over the five years leading up to 2019, more than 1,600 people in Maine died from drug overdoses. We were losing a person every day. About 8% of all babies in Maine were born substance-exposed—that's three each day. The life-saving drug Naloxone was not generally available. There were few treatment beds, and when someone was ready to get into recovery, even fewer treatment options were available if they didn't have health insurance.

When I took office, I knew that what Maine had been doing for so many years just wasn't working. We needed a coordinated response that broke down the silos of government, set aside the stigma, and spoke out about every aspect of the opioid epidemic. I promised that we would put the full force of my Administration behind the families who lost loved ones, the businesses who lost employees, and all the communities that have been diminished by this public health crisis. 

So my first executive order, signed on my first day in office, fulfilled the will of the people of Maine and expanded MaineCare to more than 90,000 people. Today, nearly 40,000 people receive treatment for substance use disorder through MaineCare. Expanding health insurance was a critical first step to confronting the opioid crisis.

I named Gordon Smith as my Director of Opioid Response, and I signed the second executive order with basic strategies and specific action steps. That order established a Prevention and Recovery Cabinet made up of commissioners from 14 government agencies and the Attorney General's Office and the Judicial Branch.

We outlined key steps to preventing overdoses and deaths, including making Naloxone widely available statewide, and since early 2019, we've distributed more than 870,000 doses of Naloxone, which has saved thousands of lives.

We then outlined steps to expand effective treatment and recovery measures, including training 250 recovery coaches and funding recovery coaches in ten emergency departments. Now we've trained more than 4,000 individuals as recovery coaches, and we've increased the number of certified recovery residences from 11 to 119.

We've created youth recovery coaching programs in Hancock and Washington counties in the schools, creating peer-to-peer connections that can give a young person the hope to face the future. And we held statewide trainings and leadership conferences, which taught more than 400 youth how to create positive change in their communities. 

We created TreatmentConnection.com, a one-stop-shop for individuals seeking treatment that allows them to find out in real time what there is available for behavioral health services among more than 500 providers. Since that went live in 2025, TreatmentConnection has been used 8,000 times.

We're also increasing good-paying jobs for people in recovery, rewarding businesses who understand the unique experiences of people in recovery. And we've created the Recovery Friendly Workplaces designation, a certification held by 86 businesses who employ nearly 25,000 people statewide.

You know, we're not giving up on interdiction as well, making sure we take drugs off the street as much as possible to keep people from becoming addicted in the first place. My Administration is doing what we can in a responsible manner to stop deadly drugs from reaching Maine, to prevent substance abuse in the first place, to treat it when we can't prevent it, to set people on a lifelong path to recovery, and, above all else, to save lives.

From January to June of this year, fatal overdoses decreased by nearly 9% in Maine. This is the fourth consecutive year of declining overdose deaths. And that's welcome news, but we know we can't be complacent. Every overdose is a tragic and, I believe, preventable loss of a valued life. So let's all recommit to supporting people as they start, stumble, or resume their recovery, and to responding to new phases of the opioid epidemic to save lives.

This is Governor Janet Mills, and thank you for listening.

Many years of experience have demonstrated that the utility of such publication is minimal, while often causing confusion and providing misleading data.  By their very nature, complaint narratives reflect negative consumer experiences and present only one side of an issue. Publishing such narratives in the Database provides a less-than-representative sample of one-sided experiences that cannot provide consumers with a balanced and accurate view of companies’ compliance with their legal obligations.
Publishing narratives and visualizations given these deficiencies risks confusing and misleading consumers, who should otherwise be able to rely on the Bureau for authoritative information as they choose the products and services that meet their individual needs. Save-the-Date: DHHS Partner Briefing on Federal Medicaid Work Requirements and Increased Renewals

Aug 14, 2026

DHHS Partner Briefing on Federal Medicaid Work Requirements and Increased Renewals 

When: Monday, August 24, 2026, 3:00 – 4:30 PM 

Where: Virtual, please register in advance. 

You are invited to join a Maine Department of Health and Human Services (DHHS) briefing to learn about plans to implement federal changes to Medicaid (in Maine, MaineCare) eligibility that will go into effect on January 1, 2027.   

During this webinar, the DHHS Office for Family Independence (OFI) and Office of MaineCare Services (OMS) will provide an overview of upcoming changes to MaineCare eligibility for Expansion Adults: 

  • New Work Requirements;  

  • Coverage renewals every 6 months instead of every 12 months; and 

  • Retroactive coverage of 1 month instead of 3 months. 

MaineCare Expansion members are adults between 19 and 64 years old who get MaineCare based on their income. They do not meet the Social Security disability guidelines or have Medicare. OFI and OMS will also provide an update on planning for implementation and communications.   

We are also pleased to share the Partner Communications Toolkit, which can be found at MaineCare.gov/work. This toolkit includes materials you can download and print or include in your digital and social media channels to reach the populations in your community that will need to know more and take action to meet the new federal Work Requirements for Medicaid.  

Important Timelines to Note:  

  • August 14, 2026: Launch of Federal Changes and Work Requirements webpages, and Partner Toolkit launch – first phase  

  • August 24, 2026: Partner briefing focused on what to know 

  • Beginning August 19, 2026: OFI will send knowledge building letters and text messages to MaineCare Expansion Adults 

  • Fall 2026: Continued communication and partnership with providers and community partners.  

  • Late 2026 and through 2027: OFI will provide direct 1:1 phone call outreach to impacted MaineCare Expansion Adults ahead of their renewal month. 

  • January 2027 and forward: MaineCare Expansion Adults will need to meet Work Requirements starting with their first renewal in 2027 and will have 6-month renewals from that point on. 

Register and join to learn more and assist with sharing information and resources in your community.     

After registering, you will receive a confirmation email containing information about joining the meeting. Feel free to share this invitation with other interested organizations who may wish to attend.   

Space is limited, so please register early.

items.content_text: This final rule requires that a State Medicaid plan must provide that the Medicaid agency will not make payment under the plan for sex-rejecting procedures for children under 18, and prohibits the use of Federal Medicaid dollars to fund sex-rejecting procedures for individuals under the age of 18. In addition, this final rule requires that a separate State Children's Health Insurance Program (CHIP) plan must provide that the CHIP agency will not make payment under the plan for sex-rejecting procedures for children under 19, and prohibits the use of Federal CHIP dollars to fund sex-rejecting procedures for individuals under the age of 19. For Medicaid and CHIP beneficiaries who are actively receiving cross-sex hormone therapy, State Medicaid and CHIP agencies may continue to claim Federal Financial Participation for those hormone therapy medications for a period of up to 6 months from the effective date of this final rule.

The launch of the application follows the U.S. Department of Education's publication of the final Workforce Pell regulations - https://www.ed.gov/about/news/press-release/us-department-of-education-issues-final-rule-create-new-workforce-pell-grant-program (effective July 20, 2026). Workforce Pell expands federal Pell Grant eligibility to approved short-term workforce training programs that prepare students for high-skill, high-wage, and in-demand careers. Under Workforce Pell, states are responsible for reviewing and certifying eligible programs before approval by the U.S. Department of Education.

"Workforce Pell opens the door to new education and career opportunities for more people across our state," said Vaughan Woodruff, Chair, State Workforce Development Board. "The Maine Workforce Pell program makes it easier for individuals to access those opportunities, strengthening the futures of Maine workers and Maine's businesses."

On July 30, the SWDB approved the Maine Workforce Pell Program Determination Policy - https://www.worksourcemaine.com/sites/default/files/2026-08/final-workforce-pell-determination-policy-8.11.2026.pdf , establishing the state's process for identifying, reviewing, and recommending eligible short-term workforce training programs for Workforce Pell. "Workforce Pell is an important step toward building a stronger workforce and expanding opportunities for people to gain the skills they need to succeed," said Laura Fortman, Commissioner of the Maine Department of Labor. Attention Trading Partners: Training for New MaineCare Partner Portal

Aug 12, 2026

We have previously shared that a refreshed and upgraded MIHMS, with a new “MaineCare Partner Portal,” is coming in October 2026. This will replace the current HealthPAS Online Portal. We are now inviting trading partners to register for training starting September 8, 2026 to help you prepare for the transition to the new portal.

Gainwell Technologies will be leading live virtual instructor-led training sessions. These courses will provide the knowledge and skills needed to navigate the new portal, complete daily business functions, and use new portal features. Training demonstrations, materials, and supporting resources will help participants prepare for a successful transition.

Steps you need to take to attend training

  • Review the available training topics listed below and identify the sessions that align with your role and responsibilities.
  • Use the LMS registration (instructions below) to create an account, access the training catalog, and enroll in applicable sessions.
  • Contact Gainwell (instructions below) if you need assistance.
  • Recorded sessions and other training materials will be available in the LMS after training sessions for ongoing reference.

MaineCare Partner Portal Training Sessions

Course Name

Description

ME - TPT - Migrated Trading Partner Log In and Account Maintenance Training (ILC)

Learn how to complete first-time login activities, configure multi-factor authentication (MFA), manage user accounts and permissions, perform account maintenance activities, and understand electronic data interchange (EDI) certification requirements and status monitoring. This course is only for Admin (R7) users.

ME - TPT - Trading Partner Registration and Account Maintenance Training (ILC)

Learn how to register a new Trading Partner account, complete account activation, manage users and permissions, associate providers and billing agents, navigate the portal, and maintain account information.

ME - TPT - Authorization, Referrals and Certifications Training (ILC)

Learn how to submit and manage authorizations, process referrals, monitor certification requests and statuses, and access related portal functionality.

ME - TPT - Dental Claim Entry & Claim Management Training (ILC)

Learn how to submit dental claims, monitor claim processing and status, and navigate claim-related portal functions.

ME - TPT - Institutional Claim Entry & Claim Management Training (ILC)

Learn how to submit institutional claims, monitor claim processing and status, and navigate claim-related portal functions.

ME - TPT - Professional Claim Entry & Claim Management Training (ILC)

Learn how to submit professional claims, monitor claim status, review payment information, access remittance advice, and complete related claim activities.

ME - TPT - MaineCare Partner Public Portal Training (ILC)

Learn about publicly available portal functionality, portal resources and reference materials, secure messaging, Trading Partner tools, and available resources.

 

LMS Access and Course Registration Instructions

Use the following steps to register for MaineCare Partner Portal training. Multiple sessions are available for each course to allow for scheduling flexibility.

  1. Go to the LMS registration site: https://mmislearningcenter.myabsorb.com/#/login.
  2. Sign in using your existing account or click Sign Up on the right side of the window to create a new account.
  3. If you need a new account, enter the enrollment key: De8pO9CBYXYB-aOCY8qp on the Sign Up window.
  4. Complete the required registration information to create your account. Note: You can enter your workplace address.
  5. The Learner Dashboard appears. From this window, you can access previous trainings, search for and enroll in the appropriate training sessions, and review your transcript.
  6. To locate the appropriate courses, search using “TPT” or the course name from the table above in the search bar at the top of the window or by opening the Course Catalog tile.
  7. Click Choose Session for each course you need to complete, then enroll in the session that best fits your schedule.
  8. You will receive an email confirmation regarding the success of your enrollment. Additionally, you will receive a Microsoft Teams calendar event for each session.
  9. On the day of the training, access the training via one of the following methods:
    • Access the Teams Meeting hyperlink from the course confirmation email.
    • Click the Microsoft Teams meeting hyperlink within the Outlook/Teams calendar event.
    • Access My Courses in the LMS and click the appropriate Microsoft Teams meeting hyperlink.

Do not forward meeting invitations to other attendees. Each participant must register through the LMS to receive course access, training credit, and post-training evaluation access.

We are offering optional virtual support sessions during the week of August 17, 2026 to help with LMS access and training registration and to ask questions about upcoming training topics. items.content_text:
Aug 11, 2026
In cooperation with the Maine Department of Health and Human Services’ Center for Disease Control and Prevention (Maine CDC), officials from U.S. Department of Agriculture’s (USDA) Wildlife Services will distribute oral rabies vaccine (ORV) baits this week. USDA Wildlife Services will distribute nearly 599,000 ORV baits in Aroostook County from August 12 through August 24.

In cooperation with the Maine Department of Health and Human Services’ Center for Disease Control and Prevention (Maine CDC), officials from U.S. Department of Agriculture’s (USDA) Wildlife Services will distribute oral rabies vaccine (ORV) baits this week. The baits help limit the potential for human and domestic animal exposures to the rabies virus through contact with infected wild animals.

Crews will spread the bait by air in rural areas and by vehicle in more populated areas. Each bait is a fishmeal-coated cube or sachet about one to two inches in size. Although humans and pets cannot get rabies from contact with the bait, they should not touch or move them.

While dogs may get upset stomachs if they eat a lot of bait, there are no known long-term health risks. If a person has skin contact with a bait cube or sachet, rinse the affected area with warm water and soap. Since 2003, the USDA’s Wildlife Services has worked to halt the spread of raccoon rabies in northern Maine. They also collaborate with Canadian officials in New Brunswick and Quebec to reduce the presence of rabies across Maine and Canada. The ORV bait distribution program in Maine is part of a larger effort by the USDA’s Wildlife Services to prevent the westward spread of raccoon rabies. This effort creates a barrier along the Appalachian Mountains from the Canadian border to Alabama.

Rabies is a virus that infects the nervous system of humans and other mammals. It spreads mainly through a bite from an infected animal. Once symptoms develop, rabies is almost always fatal. Timely post-exposure treatment can prevent disease in people. Approximately 90 percent of reported animal rabies cases in the U.S. occur in wildlife. As of August 10, 2026, 28 animals tested positive for rabies this year in 12 counties across Maine. These animals include raccoons, skunks, foxes, bats, and a goat.

To help protect yourself and your pet against rabies:

  • Keep your pets and livestock up to date on rabies vaccinations.
  • Feed pets indoors.
  • Keep garbage cans or other sources of food tightly secured.
  • Do not feed, touch, or adopt wild animals. Be cautious of stray dogs and cats.
  • Do not move wildlife. This can spread rabies into new areas.
  • Wash bite or scratch wounds with soap and water for 10 to 15 minutes.

Who to contact:

  • If an animal bites or scratches you, contact a health care provider.
  • If an animal bites or scratches your pet, contact your veterinarian.
  • To report a dead or suspicious-acting animal in northern Maine, contact the USDA’s Wildlife Services. In other parts of Maine, contact the nearest Maine Regional Communications Dispatch Center.

items.title: Maine CDC: Childhood Vaccine Guidance Remains Unchanged Following Federal Action — Maine Department of Health and Human Services News
items.content_text:
Aug 11, 2026
Maine will continue to follow the guidance of the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) on childhood vaccine recommendations, despite President Donald Trump’s executive order on childhood vaccinations, per the Maine Department of Health and Human Services’ Center for Disease Control and Prevention (Maine CDC).
“President Trump and Secretary Kennedy are playing politics with the lives of our nation’s children. Vaccines are safe and effective and save lives,”
said Governor Janet Mills.
“Maine will continue to follow the science and the facts, and our approach to vaccines remains unchanged by yesterday’s executive order.”
“Vaccines are our most effective defense against vaccine-preventable illnesses,”
said Dr. Puthiery Va, Director of the Maine CDC.
“In Maine, vaccines remain available at no cost to eligible children through the Maine CDC’s Immunization Program. Maine’s school and child care immunization requirements remain unchanged by federal actions to date.”
As the AAP has noted in their 8/10
statement
in response to this executive order:
“Vaccine recommendations from the American Academy of Pediatrics are tailored to the health of children living in the United States and are based on decades of research and systematic tracking of real-world experiences. Pediatricians recommend children receive certain vaccines at specific ages based on when children's immune systems will respond best and when they are most vulnerable to certain diseases. Sometimes this means children will receive a single shot that protects against multiple diseases, or they may receive multiple vaccines at one visit.”
Beginning in 2021, Maine removed non-medical exemptions from the school and child care immunization requirements pursuant
Public Law 2019, Ch. 154
. That decision was upheld by a vote of 72.81 percent of Maine voters at the ballot box in 2020.

items.title: US Department of Labor finds urgent care employer failed to pay over $113K in owed wages to workers for required orientation, meetings, training — U.S. Department of Labor — News Releases
items.content_text: ATLANTA – The U.S. Department of Labor has recovered $113,199 in back wages after an investigation found a Richmond Hill urgent care facility failed to pay its workers for hours worked and retaliated against a worker for questioning its pay practices.An investigation by the department’s Wage and Hour Division found that Premier Health Consultants LLC – operating as St. Joseph Candler Urgent Care – violated the Fair Labor Standards Act by paying straight time instead of time and one-half in overtime for all hours worked over 40 when employees were required to attend mandatory orientation, meetings, and training. The employer also required certain employees to work off the clock, resulting in unpaid overtime, and suspended a worker who questioned pay practices, all violations of the FLSA.Workers and employers can call the Wage and Hour Division with questions and requests for compliance assistance at its toll-free helpline, 866-4US-WAGE (487-9243). Employers are encouraged to use the agency’s industry-specific compliance assistance toolkits to learn about their responsibilities under the laws enforced by the division. The agency’s PAID program offers employers an opportunity to self-report and resolve potential minimum wage and overtime violations under the FLSA, as well as certain potential violations under the Family and Medical Leave Act. Learn more about the Wage and Hour Division, including a search tool that workers can use if they think they may be owed back wages collected by the division. Download the agency’s free timesheet app for iOS and Android devices to track hours and pay.

Hello, this is Governor Janet Mills, and thank you for listening.

Well, you know, one of the lessons learned from the pandemic time was how dependent we are as a state and community on producers from other states and other countries for basic goods like food, textiles, and construction materials. It occurred to me that our growing season is too incredibly short for us to become as self-reliant as we should be.

And after the pandemic disrupted markets and caused food shortages nationwide, we realized it was very important to have locally grown, fresh food right here in Maine and help our local farmers. So I used federal funding through my Jobs and Recovery Plan to provide grants to farmers to buy equipment to meet that higher demand for locally grown food, and I began to look for other ways to extend our growing season here in Maine.

Well, one of the things you can do is to provide greenhouses to communities who are able to support them and help people of all ages learn how to grow their own food. I called on the Legislature to provide one-time funds through the state biennial budget to buy greenhouses for as many schools and communities as possible. That will strengthen our supply of local food and will teach kids and families to grow their own food and extend the growing season.

The Legislature funded that proposal, and I'm proud to announce that we're now awarding grants to communities across Maine to expand their local food production and education programs through durable shared-use greenhouses. These grants were awarded through a competitive process. The organizations applied for them, and they include the Alfond Youth and Community Center in Waterville, where they're going to install a greenhouse to expand local food production and youth education. 

The Healthy Island Project in Stonington will use a greenhouse to increase access to fresh, locally grown food. And the Portland Community Squash will install a greenhouse to send more fresh produce home to low-income families and teach Portland Public School students how to grow their own food. Limestone Community School will install a greenhouse to expand their outdoor science program and provide students with hands on learning in nutrition, agriculture, and environmental science. And they'll run a student-run farmers market—I think that's great.

Over the past eight years, my Administration has invested more than $60 million in Maine farms and local agriculture, supporting the purchase of locally grown food, helping farmers expand their operations and equipment, strengthening our food system, and keeping Maine's farming heritage thriving.

You know, my grandparents were potato farmers in Ashland. I hope they would be proud that their granddaughter insisted that the state budget include a small amount of money for community greenhouses across the state. Sort of like the Victory Gardens of World War II and decades past, places where people of all ages can learn something about nutrition and how to grow lettuce, peppers, and parsley; where the older folks can teach the younger folks about the value of homegrown tomatoes and cucumbers and such and talk with each other in community. Where they can feel the joy of growing their own healthy food and appreciate what their neighbors are doing and appreciate their own Maine roots, the way I appreciate mine.

Dave Mallett, one of my good friends, the singer who passed away last year, used to sing a very popular song: "Inch by inch, row by row. Gonna make this garden grow. All it takes is a rake and a hoe and a piece of fertile ground."

Well, we're going to have everybody singing those songs in Maine in honor of Dave Mallett, and in honor of our agricultural heritage and the state of Maine's ability to become independent and self-reliant by community greenhouses.

This is Governor Janet Mills, and thank you for listening.

Breaking: Active Cyber Breaches Affecting Public Water Systems Demand Immediate Action.

The US EPA, FBI, Cybersecurity & Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), and Water Information Sharing & Analysis Center (WaterISAC) have held urgent briefings regarding active and on-going cybersecurity breaches at dozens of Public Water Systems (PWSs) in at least seven states across the U.S. The targeted PWSs range in size from small to large.

Many wastewater systems use similar technology as found in the drinking water sector. A common symptom of these breaches includes a loss of PLC connectivity with devices. These incidents all involve vulnerabilities related to PLCs, as described in the Iranian-Affiliated Cyber Actors Exploit Programmable Logic Controllers Across US Critical Infrastructure advisory (PDF).

The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) has information and guidance regarding malicious cyber actors targeting PLCs.

Addition of the TH Modifier to Support National Maternity Care Coding and Reimbursement Changes Effective September 1, 2026

Aug 06, 2026

The American Medical Association (AMA) announced maternity care services code changes that will be effective January 1, 2027. These changes include the removal of 17 billing codes, the addition of 12 billing codes, and revisions to 6 billing codes to reflect modern obstetric practices, allow for more accurate and transparent reporting, and to create a data foundation to better attribute maternal care and support the complexities of team-based care throughout a patient's journey.

In preparation for these changes, MaineCare is also making changes to coding requirements for maternity care services, including the transition to non-global and non-bundled care coding and reimbursement. To ensure consistent reimbursement MaineCare is directing providers to take the following actions no later than prior to September 1, 2026:

  • Adjust maternity care visit billing from global or bundled service codes to Evaluation and Management (E/M) service codes based on each member’s estimated due date and the anticipated number of visits for the remainder of their antepartum period in accordance with AMA Antepartum Transition Reporting guidance;.
  • Append the TH modifier for all maternity care E/M service codes on your claim to identify the visit as a maternity care service;
  • Transition from total-visit tracking to individual encounter documentation, as each prenatal and postpartum visit must now independently support standard E/M complexity or time rules; and
  • Monitor professional guidance from organizations like the American College of Obstetrics and Gynecology and the AMA to prepare billers and systems for the significant coding changes to be effective on January 1, 2027.

As a reminder, providers should also continue to identify and report maternity-related diagnosis codes on all claims submitted to MaineCare, as applicable, to ensure more accurate and transparent data relating to maternity services.

Competitive Skills Scholarship Program (CSSP) Rule Changes Effective August 2, 2026

August 5, 2026

The Maine Department of Labor has updated the Competitive Skills Scholarship Program (CSSP) rules to implement recent statutory changes, expand participant supports, improve program flexibility, and clarify program requirements. The revised rules took effect on August 2, 2026.

Some of the most significant changes include:

  • Expanded monthly stipend eligibility. More students may now qualify for a monthly CSSP stipend because income eligibility limits have increased.
  • Partial stipends for part-time students. Eligible part-time students may now receive a prorated monthly stipend based on their enrollment status and income.
  • Expanded support services. Eligible participants may qualify for increased assistance with transportation, vehicle repairs, and other necessary needs under higher support service funding limits.
  • Expanded educational opportunities. Eligibility has also been expanded for applicants with pre-existing preparatory associate degree programs.
  • Improved program clarity and accessibility. The revised rules simplify eligibility requirements, clarify appeal rights, improve communication preferences, and increase transparency regarding the High-Wage, In-Demand Occupations list.
  • New CSSP Cohort funding opportunities. Training providers and their partners will be invited to apply for CSSP Cohort funding. The Maine Department of Labor will host a listening session to gather feedback on implementation before issuing a Request for Applications (RFA) for pilot cohort programs.

For those interested in reviewing the complete rule changes, including the final adopted rule, tracked changes, and the Department's Summary of Comments and Responses from the rulemaking process, please visit the Maine Department of Labor Rulemaking webpage: https://www.maine.gov/labor/rulemaking/

CSSP Cohort Listening Session

Community members interested in learning more about the CSSP Cohort model are invited to join a listening session on September 18th, at 10:00 a.m. to share ideas, discuss opportunities to expand access, and help identify implementation priorities.

Zoom Registration: https://mainestate.zoom.us/meeting/register/-vPlt9ZbSG23mGKG96bmsg

Current CSSP participants will receive a separate email describing the rule changes and inviting them to schedule a meeting with their CSSP case manager to review whether they may qualify for additional benefits under the new rules.

Thank you for your continued partnership in helping Maine people access education, training, and employment through the Competitive Skills Scholarship Program.

Important Information Regarding Cancellation of Certificate of Title:

Pursuant to Title 29-A, section §669, beginning on July 29, 2026, residents of the state of Maine are able to request cancellation of their Certificate of Title for Tiny Home or Manufactured Home for purposes of obtaining residential real property.


When a Tiny Home or Manufactured Home is permanently affixed to land that you own, or land where you have permission from the land owner via a signed sworn statement, you may request to cancel the Certificate of Title. Once the Certificate of Title is cancelled, the home becomes part of the residential real property instead of being treated as personal property. Under Maine law, this process is handled through the county Registry of Deeds and the Maine Secretary of State Bureau of Motor Vehicles.
 

How to Cancel your Certificate of Tittle for Tiny Home or Manufactured Home 

Before requesting cancellation of the title, make sure:

  • You own both the manufactured home or tiny home and the land where it is located; and/or
  • The individual that owns the property has given a sworn signed statement of authorization.
  • The home has been permanently affixed to the property in accordance with Maine law.
  • Any existing liens have been released or the lienholder has agreed to release the lien upon cancellation of the title.

  • This process is not for double-wide mobile homes/trailers

1. Gather the required documentation

You will need to obtain the following documents before submitting your request:

  • The Original Certificate of Title
  • A description of the home, including;
    • Model Year
    • Manufacturer {make}
    • Width
    • Length
    • Identification Number/Serial Number
  • Lien Release Documentation, if applicable
  • The legal description of the real property
  • A sworn statement confirming:
    • You own both the land, and the Tiny Home or Manufactured Home, or a sworn statement from the property land owner
    • The home is permanently affixed to the property/ground

If you are unable to locate your current Certificate of Title for Tiny Home or Manufactured Home, you are able to request a duplicate title by printing off the Duplicate Title Request Application {MVT-8} and mailing it into our Bureau of Motor Vehicles office with a $33 check-or-moneyorder payable to "Secretary of State". Once a duplicate title is obtained, you wll then be able to continue to the next step.
2. Record the appropriate documents with the Registry of Deeds

Take all the above documents listed to the Registry of Deeds in the county where the property is located. The Registry of Deeds will record the documents as part of the public land records.

For further information on the nearest Registry of Deeds and other contact information, please Maine Registry of Deeds 

3. Submit the Request for Cancellation of Certificate of Title

After the documents above have been recorded, submit a completed Cancellation Request form {MVT-51} and provide all original documentation that was recorded within the Registry of Deeds {photocopies are not accepted}. Be sure to include the Book and Page number from the prior step from the Registry of Deeds

4. Receive Confirmation and record Cancellation Letter document with Registry of Deeds

Once the Secretary of State reviews and approves your request, you will be mailed a Cancellation Letter stating the process is complete. You must then have the Cancellation Letter document recorded within the county Registry of Deeds. This is a crucial step, as the application process is pending the verification of receipt and recording at the Registry of Deeds office.

5. Return proof of recording to the Bureau of Motor Vehicles

As mentioned above, this process is dependent on the documentation within the public record of the residential real property. Once that document has been recorded within the Registry of Deeds, please return proof of filing with the Bureau of Motor Vehicles via email, both of which are listed below;

Email: titles.bmv@maine.gov

Disclaimer: This information is intended as a general overview of the Maine titling process for Tiny Homes and Manufactured Homes. Requirements may vary depending on the circumstances of the transaction. For further information, please contact the Title Services Division at 207-624-9000 extension 52138, Monday through Friday 08:30AM to 4:30PM

Public Guidance Statement RE: HUD's New Emotional Support Animal Enforcement Guidance and 
Maine Housing Providers' Continuing Obligations Under the Maine Human Rights Act 
August 4, 2026 
What Has Changed at the Federal Level 
On May 22, 2026, the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) issued an enforcement 
memorandum announcing that it will no longer find reasonable cause in housing complaints involving 
emotional support animals (ESAs). In other words, animals that provide comfort, companionship, or otherwise 
mitigate the effects of a person’s disability but have not been individually trained to perform specific 
disability-related tasks are no longer protected at the federal level. Going forward, HUD will pursue 
enforcement only where an animal has been trained to perform work or tasks directly related to a person's 
disability (essentially, HUD has imported the Americans with Disabilities Act's narrower "service animal" 
definition into Fair Housing Act enforcement). 
HUD simultaneously rescinded its 2020 guidance, which had for years provided meaningful protections to 
individuals who rely on ESAs as part of their disability-related care. After 35 years without updating its 
regulations in this area, the federal government's chosen solution has been, perhaps unsurprisingly, to reduce 
protections rather than clarify them. 
The Maine Human Rights Commission takes note of this development. We also take note that it changes 
nothing in Maine.

Maine State Revised Statues Website 

Property Definitions 

This section provides information to help homeowners, buyers, and other interested parties understand the types of construction, material, and installation that classify each type of home. By outlining these definitions. Read through the below definitions for the appropriate boxes to get more information.

Tiny Home Definition

Pursuant to Maine Statute 29-A, section §101, subsection 80-C, Maine's definition of a "Tiny Home" is a living space permanently constructed on a frame or chassis and designed for use as permanent living quarters that: 

  • Complies with American National Standards Institute standard A 119.5 on plumbing, propane, fire and life safety and construction or National Fire Protection Association standard 1192 on plumbing, propane and fire and life safety for recreational vehicles; 
  • Does not exceed 400 sq. feet in size; 
  • Does not exceed any dimension allowed for operation on a public way; 

  • Is a vehicle without motive power. 

Manufactured Home Definition

Pursuant to Maine Statute 29-A, section §101, subsection 32-B, Maine's definition of a "Manufactured Home" is a structural unit or units designed to be used as a dwelling or dwellings and constructed in a manufacturing facility and then transported by the use of its own chassis or placement on an independent chassis to a building site. 

"Manufactured housing" includes any type of building that is constructed at a manufacturing facility and then transported to a building site where it is used for housing and that may be purchased, sold, offered for sale or brokered by a licensee in the interim. Three types of manufactured housing are included: 

  • Units constructed after June 15, 1976; 
  • State-certified modular homes; 
  • Units constructed prior to June 15, 1976

How to Title your Tiny Home or Manufactured Home

A Certificate of Title establishes legal ownership of a Tiny Home or Manufactured Home in the State of Maine. The application process varies depending on whether the home is new or used and the year of the model. Beginning in 2009, The Bureau of Motor Vehicles began issuing titles for Manufactured Homes and in 2019, the Bureau of Motor Vehicles began issuing titles for Tiny Homes. 

Note: If the manufactured homeowner is deceased, additional documentation may be required depending on the circumstances. Please contact the Bureau of Motor Vehicles, before submitting your application.

1. Determine if the model year is eligible for a Certificate of Title

The following information regarding the home’s year and housing status will help determine which model years are eligible for a Certificate of Title.

  • Manufactured Home: The Secretary of State may issue a Certificate of Title for new or used manufactured housing that was previously issued a State of Maine Certificate of Title, or a model year 2007-or-later model that was never issued a Certificate of Title. 
     
  • Tiny Home: The Secretary of State shall issue certificates of title for new tiny homes beginning with model year 2020. The Secretary of State shall issue a Certificate of Title for a used tiny home of any model year that was previously issued a State of Maine Certificate of Title.
     
2. Identify who must apply for a Certificate of Title and what documents are required

There are generally four categories of individuals who may submit an application for a Certificate of Title. The submission process and required documentation may vary depending on whether the application is completed by the customer or the retail seller/dealer. Please refer to the document list below:

New home purchased from a Maine dealer: The retail seller submits the following:

items.title: US Department of Labor finds child labor and wage violations  at 3 San Antonio bakery and café locations — U.S. Department of Labor — News Releases
items.content_text: SAN ANTONIO – The U.S. Department of Labor has recovered thousands in back wages and assessed penalties after a federal investigation revealed child labor, minimum wage, and overtime violations by the operators of three La Panaderia Bakery & Café locations in San Antonio.The department’s Wage and Hour Division investigated the pay practices of Tequila Almond Croissant LLC, Pan Dulce LLC, and SA Bakery Co. LLC. All three do business as La Panaderia Bakery & Café in San Antonio with locations at 301 E. Houston Street; 17030 Fiesta Texas Drive; and 8305 Broadway.Division investigators found the employers violated child labor provisions of the Fair Labor Standards Act. Specifically, they employed a 13-year-old minor who was under the legal age for employment and permitted a 15-year-old minor to work overnight, which is prohibited for 14- and 15-year-olds. The division assessed a $25,706 civil money penalty for the child labor violations.The division’s investigation also revealed minimum wage violations due to the employers’ failure to pay one worker for two overnight shifts at the La Cantera café location on Fiesta Texas Drive. The employers also failed to combine hours for employees who worked at multiple café locations and paid the employees straight-time rates instead of the required time-and-one-half overtime rates. Employers and workers can contact the division with questions and requests for compliance assistance at its toll-free helpline, 866-4US-WAGE (487-9243). Employers are also encouraged to use the agency’s industry-specific compliance assistance toolkits to learn about their responsibilities under the laws enforced by the division. The agency’s PAID program offers employers an opportunity to self-report and resolve potential minimum wage and overtime violations under the FLSA, as well as certain potential violations under the Family and Medical Leave Act.Download the agency’s free timesheet app for iOS and Android devices to track hours and pay.

items.title: Magnuson-Stevens Fishery Conservation and Management Act Provisions; Fisheries of the Northeastern United States; Northeast Multispecies Fishery; Framework Adjustment 72 — Federal Register — Documents Matching 'Maine'
items.content_text: NMFS issues this interim final rule to implement Framework Adjustment 72 (Framework 72) to the Northeast Multispecies Fishery Management Plan (FMP), specifically to implement status determination criteria for Georges Bank yellowtail flounder, set catch limits for multispecies (groundfish) stocks, and revise the process for setting recreational measures for Atlantic cod and haddock. This action is necessary to respond to updated scientific information and to achieve the goals and objectives of the FMP. The measures are intended to help prevent overfishing, rebuild overfished stocks, achieve optimum yield, and ensure that management measures are based on the best scientific information available.
